This lands first on the dispatcher: he took shared money without consent and only returned it when challenged, so his reliability is in question. It lands on the coworkers: their gift money and their ability to work together are at risk. It lands on the person leaving, who is not in the room but would be harmed if the collection is mishandled or the farewell becomes a quarrel. It lands on you: you have to keep working with him, and your anger is understandable but can push you toward public punishment rather than protection. Your role as coworker obliges you to look after shared money and to speak plainly to the person whose conduct threatens it, not to humiliate him or pretend nothing happened. You are entitled to raise the issue, but the entitlement does not make a public call-out the right use of it. The conduct was wrong even if repaid: taking what belongs to everyone requires consent, and returning it after being cornered does not instantly rebuild trust. Watch your own motive: if you want the team to see him lose, that is not about safety. The aim should be repair: keep the gift money safe, give him a chance to act honestly under clear limits, and preserve the working relationship for the rest of the shift.

Don't make it a team announcement, and don't swallow it either. Those are not the only choices.

Trust asks whether someone is reliable now, and that has to be shown, not assumed because the money was returned.

For the rest of the shift, work with him normally on logs and breaks. Be civil, be exact, and do not bring it up again in front of the team. Later, when things are calm, you can say one clear sentence about the tin: 'If you need something from shared cash, ask first; otherwise it can't happen.' The goal is not to prove he is bad, but to make the money safe, let him repair his standing by acting honestly, and keep the shift workable.
